In Listening to Prestige, Tad Richards tells the label's story through many of its most important recordings.
By the mid-1950s, Prestige had become one of the most important independent labels in jazz, documenting the transition from bebop to hard bop and beyond. Listening To Prestige grew out of a project Richards began years earlier when he decided to listen his way through the Prestige catalog. What

...

As Richards explains, the idea was simple: listen to the catalog and see whether those classic Prestige recordings really held up as well as memory suggested.
Many listeners associate Prestige Records with a sense of spontaneity and improvisation. Richards captures that spirit well, guiding readers through sessions that reflect the changing sound of jazz from the bebop era through the 1960s. Richards's idea grew out of conversations with friends who were also jazz fans, wondering how well the Prestige catalog really held up.

...

This gave Richards the opportunity to revisit many classic sessions featuring artists such as Sonny Rollins, Miles Davis, the Modern Jazz Quartet, Yusef Lateef and Eric Dolphy.

Book Review: Listening to Prestige

One potential function of a book-length treatment of a subject is as a springboard to initiate a wider discussion.

...

even dig deeply into) the work of artists who recorded for that label.
And that is part of what Tad Richards does with his wonderful Listening to Prestige . On one level, it’s an appreciation – a love letter, if you will – of Bob Weinstock’s influential independent record label. But simultaneously, Listening t o Prestige provides a canvas upon which Richards places the work of many – not quite all, but close – of the era’s jazz artists into a larger context.

...

And within each chapter are sidebars – sometimes lengthy, sometimes brief – in which Richards takes a more personal look at specific records. (Hence the “Listening to…” of the book’s title.) Readers largely unfamiliar with the jazz canon of the era may initially find themselves slightly overwhelmed by the sheer volume of names therein, but Richards’ clear, concise and accessible writing style all but guarantees that those readers will nonetheless be drawn in by his work.
Along with providing context that helps elucidate the work that those artists did for Prestige – whether it’s a big name like Miles Davis , Sonny Rollins or John Coltrane , or a relative obscurity like vibraphonist Dave Pike (a favorite of mine, by the way) – Richards helps the reader understand why what they did is worth a listen.
